coverage: Both full English editions. BOOKS 1-2 (Clio and Euterpe, sections 1-397) are authored; Books 3-9 are in progress. Named people and named peoples. Cities, rivers, mountains, seas and countries are not cast.

entities.name: Croesus
entities.body: King of Lydia, the first barbarian Herodotus knows of to subdue Greeks. He asks Solon who is the happiest of men, loses his son, attacks Persia on a misread oracle, loses his kingdom, and ends as Cyrus’s adviser.

entities.name: Candaules
entities.body: The last Heraclid king of Sardis, so convinced of his wife’s beauty that he made his bodyguard look at her naked — and was killed for it. The Greeks call him Myrsilus.

entities.name: Gyges
entities.body: Candaules’s favourite spearman, forced by the queen to choose between dying and killing his king. He took the kingdom, and the Delphic oracle confirmed it — adding that the Heraclids would be avenged in the fifth generation.

entities.name: Ardys
entities.body: Gyges’s son and successor, who took Priene and attacked Miletus, and in whose reign the Cimmerians took Sardis.

entities.name: Sadyattes
entities.body: Ardys’s son, who began the long war against Miletus.

entities.name: Alyattes
entities.body: Croesus’s father, who inherited the Milesian war, burnt the temple of Athena of Assesos by accident, fell ill, and made peace on the oracle’s terms.

entities.name: Atys
entities.body: Croesus’s able son, whom Croesus dreamed would die by an iron point — and who died on a boar hunt, by the spear of the guest he had been given as a guard.

entities.name: Atys
entities.body: The ancient king from whose son Lydus the Lydian people took their name — a different man from Croesus’s son, five hundred years earlier.

entities.name: Pantaleon
entities.body: Croesus’s half-brother by a different mother, whom one faction tried to make king; Croesus had the man who tried it dragged over a carding-comb.

entities.name: The Heraclids
entities.body: The line descended from Heracles that ruled Sardis for twenty-two generations before Gyges.

entities.name: The Mermnadae
entities.body: The family of Gyges and Croesus, which took the Lydian throne from the Heraclids.

entities.name: Alcaeus
entities.body: Son of Heracles, and the ancestor the Heraclid kings of Sardis traced themselves to.

entities.name: Agron
entities.body: Son of Ninus, the first of the Heraclids to become king of Sardis.

entities.name: Ninus
entities.body: Agron’s father, in the Heraclid genealogy.

entities.name: Belus
entities.body: Ninus’s father in the same genealogy; the older translation spells him Belos.

entities.name: Myrsus
entities.body: Candaules’s father.

entities.name: Lydus
entities.body: Son of Atys, from whom the Lydians took their name; they had been called Meonians.

entities.name: Adrastus
entities.body: A Phrygian prince who had killed his own brother by accident, was purified by Croesus, was given charge of Croesus’s son, killed him by accident too, and cut his own throat on the grave.

entities.name: Hyroeades
entities.body: The Mardian soldier who watched a Lydian climb down the unguarded cliff after a fallen helmet, and so found the way into Sardis.

entities.name: Pactyas
entities.body: The Lydian left in charge of Croesus’s gold, who used it to raise a revolt against Cyrus and then fled from city to city until the Chians sold him for a stretch of land.

entities.name: Cyrus
entities.body: Cyrus the Great: the grandson Astyages tried to have killed, raised by a herdsman, who overthrew the Medes, took Sardis and Babylon, and died fighting Tomyris beyond the Araxes.

entities.name: Astyages
entities.body: The last king of the Medes, who dreamed twice about his daughter, ordered his grandson killed, served Harpagos his own son at dinner, and lost his kingdom to the grandson who survived.

entities.name: Harpagos
entities.body: Astyages’s kinsman, ordered to expose the infant Cyrus and unable to do it. Astyages fed him his own son for it; Harpagos waited years and then handed Astyages’s army to Cyrus. He afterwards conquered Ionia for Persia. The two editions spell him Harpagos and Harpagus.

entities.name: Deioces
entities.body: The Mede who made himself indispensable as a judge, was elected king, built Agbatana with its seven coloured walls, and made himself invisible to his subjects on purpose.

entities.name: Phraortes
entities.body: Deioces’s son, who subdued the Persians and died attacking the Assyrians of Nineveh.

entities.name: Cyaxares
entities.body: Phraortes’s son, who first organised the Median army into companies, besieged Nineveh, and was interrupted by the Scythians for twenty-eight years.

entities.name: Mandane
entities.body: Astyages’s daughter and Cyrus’s mother, married off to a quiet Persian because of what her father dreamed about her.

entities.name: Cambyses
entities.body: Cyrus’s father — a Persian of good family whom Astyages judged harmless. Not the Cambyses who succeeds Cyrus.

entities.name: Cambyses
entities.body: Cyrus’s son, to whom Cyrus handed Croesus and the kingdom before riding against the Massagetai. Book 3 is largely his.

entities.name: Mitradates
entities.body: The herdsman ordered to expose the infant Cyrus, whose own newborn son had just died; his wife asked for the living child instead.

entities.name: Kyno
entities.body: The herdsman’s wife, called Spako in Median and Kyno in Greek — both meaning "dog", which is how the story of the infant Cyrus being suckled by a bitch got started.

entities.name: Artembares
entities.body: The Mede whose son was whipped by the boy Cyrus playing at being king — the complaint that made Astyages look at the boy’s face.

entities.name: Mazares
entities.body: The Mede sent to put down Pactyas and reduce the Ionians; he died in the middle of it.

entities.name: Tabalos
entities.body: The Persian left as governor of Sardis, besieged in the acropolis by Pactyas.

entities.name: Darius
entities.body: Darius son of Hystaspes, later king of Persia, who appears in Book 1 only as the young man in Cyrus’s dream and as the future plunderer of a Babylonian statue. The two editions spell him Darius and Dareios.

entities.name: Hystaspes
entities.body: Darius’s father, a Persian in Cyrus’s army whom Cyrus sent home to watch his son after the dream.

entities.name: Tomyris
entities.body: Queen of the Massagetai, who refused Cyrus’s offer of marriage, warned him to keep to his own country, lost her son to his trick with the wine, and put his head in a skin of blood so that he could drink his fill.

entities.name: Spargapises
entities.body: Tomyris’s son, taken by Cyrus’s stratagem with the feast and the unmixed wine, who asked to be unbound and killed himself.

entities.name: Labynetus
entities.body: The king of Babylon, named twice — as one of the two mediators of the peace between Lydia and Media, and as the ruler Cyrus’s canals were dug against.

entities.name: Syennesis
entities.body: The Cilician, who with Labynetus mediated the peace between Alyattes and Cyaxares.

entities.name: The Magians
entities.body: One of the Median tribes, and the interpreters of dreams and portents at the Persian court; their reading of Astyages’s dream is what sets the whole story going.

entities.name: The Chaldeans
entities.body: The priests of Bel at Babylon, who told Herodotus what stood in the temple and what had been taken from it.

entities.name: Solon
entities.body: The Athenian lawgiver, who left Athens for ten years so that his laws could not be unmade, came to Sardis, and refused to call Croesus happy while he was still alive.

entities.name: Tellus
entities.body: The Athenian Solon names as the happiest of men: he lived well, saw his children’s children, and died fighting at Eleusis and was buried where he fell.

entities.name: Cleobis
entities.body: One of two Argive brothers who pulled their mother’s ox-cart to the temple of Hera; she prayed for the best thing a man can have, and they died in their sleep.

entities.name: Biton
entities.body: Cleobis’s brother, named with him as second happiest.

entities.name: Peisistratus
entities.body: Tyrant of Athens three times over: once by wounding himself and getting a bodyguard, once with a tall woman dressed as Athena riding into the city beside him, and once by force and mercenaries.

entities.name: Megacles
entities.body: Son of Alcmaeon and leader of the faction of the shore, who brought Peisistratus back to Athens by marrying him to his daughter, and drove him out again when the marriage displeased him.

entities.name: Lycurgus
entities.body: Son of Aristolaides and leader of the faction of the plain — the Athenian rival of Megacles and Peisistratus, not the Spartan lawgiver of the next few pages.

entities.name: Alcmaeon
entities.body: Megacles’s father, named in the Athenian faction fighting.

entities.name: Hippocrates
entities.body: Peisistratus’s father.

entities.name: Lygdamis
entities.body: The Naxian who gave Peisistratus money and men for his third return, and was set up as tyrant of Naxos for it.

entities.name: Lycurgus
entities.body: The lawgiver who gave Sparta its whole constitution — brought from Crete, or given by the Pythia, depending on who is telling it — and turned the worst-governed Greeks into the best.

entities.name: Leon
entities.body: A king of Sparta in the generation before Anaxandrides, under whom the Spartans beat everyone except Tegea.

entities.name: Hegesicles
entities.body: Leon’s fellow-king at Sparta.

entities.name: Anaxandrides
entities.body: King of Sparta at the time of Croesus’s embassy.

entities.name: Ariston
entities.body: Anaxandrides’s fellow-king at Sparta when Croesus sent for an alliance.

entities.name: Lichas
entities.body: One of the Spartan "Well-doers", who found the bones of Orestes under a blacksmith’s forge at Tegea by taking the smith’s talk about a seven-foot coffin literally.

entities.name: Orestes
entities.body: Son of Agamemnon, whose bones the oracle told Sparta to fetch home from Tegea before they could beat the Tegeans.

entities.name: Agamemnon
entities.body: Orestes’s father, named in the oracle.

entities.name: Othryades
entities.body: The one Spartan left standing after the Battle of the Champions at Thyrea, who stripped the Argive dead and stayed on the field — and afterwards killed himself for shame at outliving his three hundred.

entities.name: Chilon
entities.body: The Spartan sage who warned Hippocrates, after the cauldron boiled over without a fire, not to have a son.

entities.name: Periander
entities.body: Tyrant of Corinth, son of Cypselus, who tortured the crew that had thrown Arion overboard, and who took his lesson in government from Thrasybulus’s walk through a cornfield.

entities.name: Cypselus
entities.body: Periander’s father and tyrant of Corinth before him; the treasury at Delphi that bears the Corinthian name is really his.

entities.name: Thrasybulus
entities.body: Tyrant of Miletus and Periander’s guest-friend, who got wind of Alyattes’s intentions and had the city’s last grain heaped in the marketplace for the herald to see.

entities.name: Arion
entities.body: The lyre-player of Methymna, robbed by his own crew, who asked to sing once more in full costume, jumped overboard, and was carried to Taenarum on a dolphin’s back.

entities.name: Thales
entities.body: Thales of Miletus, who foretold the year of the eclipse that stopped the battle between the Medes and the Lydians, and who is said to have diverted the Halys so Croesus could cross.

entities.name: Bias
entities.body: Bias of Priene, who talked Croesus out of building a fleet by telling him the islanders were buying horses — and who advised the Ionians, too late, to sail away and found one city in Sardinia.

entities.name: Pittacus
entities.body: Pittacus of Mytilene, named as the other candidate for the sage who gave Croesus the advice about the islanders and their horses.

entities.name: Aristodicos
entities.body: The man of Kyme who, told by the oracle to give up the suppliant Pactyas, walked round the temple pulling nests down from the eaves until the god objected — and then asked the god the obvious question.

entities.name: Arganthonios
entities.body: King of Tartessos, who reigned eighty years and lived a hundred and twenty, and offered the Phocaeans his whole country to settle in.

entities.name: Amasis
entities.body: King of Egypt, named in Book 1 as one of Croesus’s allies and as the man Solon visited.

entities.name: Minos
entities.body: Son of Europa, who ruled the sea in the old time and whose subjects the Carians were before they came to the mainland.

entities.name: Sarpedon
entities.body: Minos’s brother, driven out of Crete, who led the Termilai into the land that became Lycia.

entities.name: Lycos
entities.body: Son of Pandion, exiled from Athens by his brother Aegeus, from whom the Lycians took their name.

entities.name: Pandion
entities.body: Lycos’s father.

entities.name: Europa
entities.body: The king’s daughter carried off from Tyre — the second of the four abductions with which Herodotus opens the quarrel between Europe and Asia.

entities.name: Io
entities.body: Daughter of Inachus, carried off from Argos by Phoenician traders — the first abduction, and the beginning of the whole business.

entities.name: Inachus
entities.body: Io’s father, king of Argos.

entities.name: Medea
entities.body: The king of Colchis’s daughter, carried off by Greeks in a warship up the Phasis — the third abduction.

entities.name: Helen
entities.body: Carried off by Alexander, which the Persians say was the fourth abduction and the one the Greeks made a war of, for a single woman.

entities.name: Alexander
entities.body: The son of Priam — Paris — who carried off Helen because earlier abductions had gone unpunished. Not the Alexander who rules Macedon later in the Histories.

entities.name: Priam
entities.body: Alexander’s father, king of Troy.

entities.name: Midas
entities.body: King of Phrygia, son of Gordias, the only barbarian before Gyges to dedicate offerings at Delphi — his throne.

entities.name: Gordias
entities.body: Midas’s father, and also the father of the Adrastus who killed Croesus’s son.

entities.name: Amphiaraus
entities.body: The seer whose oracle Croesus tested along with the others, and to whose shrine he sent a shield and spear of solid gold. The two editions spell him Amphiaraus and Amphiaraos.

entities.name: Zeus
entities.body: Invoked in Book 1 as the Purifier, the Protector of Suppliants and the Guardian of Friendship, all three by Adrastus over the body of Croesus’s son.

entities.name: Apollo
entities.body: The god of Delphi, called Loxias where he speaks in oracles and Ismenian where Croesus sends him a tripod at Thebes. He gave Croesus three years’ grace and could not do more.

entities.name: The Pythian prophetess
entities.body: The priestess through whom Apollo answers at Delphi — who told Gyges the Heraclids would be avenged, told Croesus he would destroy a great empire, and told Sparta to fetch the bones of Orestes.

entities.name: Athena
entities.body: Athena of Assesos, whose temple Alyattes burnt by accident and had to rebuild twice before he could be cured.

entities.name: Hera
entities.body: At whose Argive festival Cleobis and Biton pulled the cart, and whose priestess prayed for the best thing a man can have.

entities.name: Aphrodite
entities.body: Worshipped as Aphrodite Urania, whose temple at Ascalon the Scythians plundered and were punished with a lasting disease; the Assyrians call her Mylitta.

entities.name: Heracles
entities.body: Ancestor, through Alcaeus, of the old kings of Sardis.

entities.name: The Persians
entities.body: Herodotus’s subject: the people whose learned men give him his opening account of the quarrel, and who under Cyrus go from subjects of the Medes to masters of Asia.

entities.name: The Lydians
entities.body: Croesus’s people, the first to strike coin and to keep retail shops, and the first barbarians the Greeks paid tribute to.

entities.name: The Medes
entities.body: The empire Cyrus overthrew, first to revolt from Assyria and first to be organised into a kingdom.

entities.name: The Ionians
entities.body: The twelve cities on the Asian coast that Croesus subdued and Cyrus took, and whose refusal to help Cyrus first cost them their liberty.

entities.name: The Aeolians
entities.body: The Greeks of the coast north of Ionia, subdued with them. The two editions spell them Aeolians and Aiolians.

entities.name: The Dorians
entities.body: The third of the three Greek divisions, of whom the five cities of the Triopian temple are the Asian branch.

entities.name: The Hellenes
entities.body: Herodotus’s word for the Greeks as one people, set against the barbarians from the first sentence of the work.

entities.name: The Athenians
entities.body: Of Pelasgian stock and never moved from their land; under Peisistratus in Croesus’s day, and the people Croesus judged the first among the Ionians.

entities.name: The Lacedaemonians
entities.body: The Spartans, whom Croesus chose as allies because they were the first of the Dorians — worst-governed of the Greeks once, and best-governed since Lycurgus.

entities.name: The Scythians
entities.body: The nomads who drove the Cimmerians out of their homes, followed them into Asia, and held the upper country for twenty-eight years before the Medes got them drunk and killed them.

entities.name: The Cimmerians
entities.body: Driven from their own land by the Scythians, they took Sardis in the reign of Ardys — all of it but the citadel.

entities.name: The Massagetai
entities.body: Tomyris’s people, beyond the Araxes: a great and warlike nation who share their wives, eat their old, and killed Cyrus.

entities.name: The Babylonians
entities.body: The people of the greatest city Herodotus knows, taken by Cyrus when he drew off the Euphrates and walked in along the riverbed while they were at a festival.

entities.name: The Assyrians
entities.body: Rulers of Upper Asia for five hundred and twenty years before the Medes revolted.

entities.name: The Phoenicians
entities.body: The traders who, in the Persian account, began the whole quarrel by carrying off Io from Argos.

entities.name: The Egyptians
entities.body: Croesus’s allies through Amasis, and a people Herodotus will spend his entire second book on.

entities.name: The Milesians
entities.body: Of Miletus: at war with Lydia for eleven years, then the only Ionians to make terms with Cyrus on the old footing.

entities.name: The Samians
entities.body: Who seized the great bronze bowl the Lacedaemonians were sending to Croesus — or bought it from the men who did, depending on which side is telling it.

entities.name: The Chians
entities.body: Who alone helped the Milesians in the Lydian war, and who afterwards dragged Pactyas out of the temple of Athena and handed him over for a piece of land.

entities.name: The Phocaeans
entities.body: The first Greeks to make long sea voyages, who sailed away from Ionia rather than submit, sank half their own fleet’s worth of enemies off Corsica, and dropped an iron bar in the sea to swear by. The two editions spell them Phocaeans and Phocaians.

entities.name: The Carians
entities.body: Once islanders and subjects of Minos, called Leleges then; they claim to be native to the mainland, and gave the Greeks the crest, the shield-grip and the blazon.

entities.name: The Caunians
entities.body: Neighbours of the Carians who say they came from Crete, and who once drove out foreign gods by beating the air with their spears as far as the border.

entities.name: The Lycians
entities.body: Sarpedon’s people, the Termilai renamed after Lycos; they reckon descent by the mother, and burnt their own women and treasure before dying on Harpagos’s swords. The two editions spell them Lycians and Lykians.

entities.name: The Pedasians
entities.body: The only people of the Halicarnassus region who gave Harpagos trouble; their priestess of Athena grows a beard when disaster is coming.

entities.name: The Pelasgians
entities.body: The people the Greeks were before they were Greeks — whose language Herodotus cannot determine except by what their descendants still speak.

entities.name: The Argives
entities.body: Cleobis and Biton’s people, and the losers of the Battle of the Champions at Thyrea.

entities.name: The Corinthians
entities.body: In whose treasury at Delphi Gyges’s gold stands — though it belongs properly to Cypselus — and who tell the story of Arion.

entities.name: The Lesbians
entities.body: Who agree with the Corinthians about Arion and the dolphin.

entities.name: The Tegeans
entities.body: The Arcadians who beat Sparta and made the prisoners work their own fields in the fetters they had brought, until the bones of Orestes changed the war.

entities.name: The Arcadians
entities.body: Acorn-eaters, whose land the Spartans asked the oracle for and did not get.

entities.name: The Delphians
entities.body: Keepers of the oracle, who tell Herodotus which offerings are whose and gave the Lydians precedence in consulting the god.

entities.name: The Cretans
entities.body: Whom Herodotus supposes to have been the crew that carried off Europa.

entities.name: The Phrygians
entities.body: Adrastus’s people, and one of the nations inside the Halys that Croesus ruled.

entities.name: The Mysians
entities.body: Of Mysian Olympus, whose boar ruined the fields and cost Croesus his son.

entities.name: The Paphlagonians
entities.body: One of the peoples inside the Halys ruled by Croesus.

entities.name: The Thracians
entities.body: The Thynian and Bithynian Thracians of Asia, among Croesus’s subjects.

entities.name: The Syrians
entities.body: The people on the Cappadocian side of the Halys, whom the Greeks call Cappadocians.

entities.name: The Armenians
entities.body: From whose mountains the Halys and the Tigris come down.

entities.name: The Matienians
entities.body: From whose mountains the Gyndes rises — the river Cyrus punished by splitting it into three hundred and sixty channels.

entities.name: The Arabians
entities.body: Who call Aphrodite Alilat, and from whom, with the Assyrians, the Persians learned to worship her.

entities.name: The Achaeans
entities.body: Who drove the Ionians out of the Peloponnese, and whose twelve districts the Ionians copied.

entities.name: The Tyrsenians
entities.body: The Etruscans, said by the Lydians to be their own emigrants, sent out under Tyrsenus when the famine had lasted eighteen years.

entities.name: The Carthaginians
entities.body: Who joined the Etruscans against the Phocaean settlers on Corsica.

entities.name: The Tartessians
entities.body: Arganthonios’s people, beyond the Pillars, with whom the Phocaeans became friends.

entities.name: The Ephesians
entities.body: The first Greeks Croesus attacked, who ran a rope from their walls to the temple of Artemis and dedicated the city to her.

entities.name: The Smyrnaeans
entities.body: Who took in the exiles from Colophon and lost their city to them at a festival outside the walls. The older translation says only “the men of Smyrna”.

entities.name: The Cymeans
entities.body: Of Kyme, who would neither give up the suppliant Pactyas nor keep him, and sent him to Mytilene instead. The older translation calls them only “the men of Kyme”.

entities.name: The Telmessians
entities.body: The interpreters of portents whom Croesus consulted about the snakes in the suburb of Sardis, and whose answer came too late.

entities.name: The Leleges
entities.body: The name the Carians went by while they were islanders and subjects of Minos.

entities.name: Min
entities.body: The first man to be king of Egypt, who dammed the Nile away from Memphis and founded the city on the reclaimed ground. The older translation spells him Men.

entities.name: Nitocris
entities.body: The one queen in the priests’ list of three hundred and thirty kings, who avenged her murdered brother by drowning his killers at a feast and then threw herself into a room full of ashes.

entities.name: Moeris
entities.body: The king before whose reign the Nile needed only eight cubits to flood Egypt, and whose name the great lake carries. The two editions spell the lake Moeris and Moiris.

entities.name: Sesostris
entities.body: The conqueror who set out with a fleet from the Arabian gulf, marched through Asia into Europe, and left carved pillars behind him — with a woman’s parts cut on them where the people gave in without a fight.

entities.name: Pheros
entities.body: Sesostris’s son, blinded for throwing a spear into the flooding Nile, and cured after ten years by a remedy that cost the lives of a great many women.

entities.name: Proteus
entities.body: The king of Memphis who held Helen and the stolen treasure in Egypt for the whole length of the Trojan war, and sent Alexander away — the story Herodotus believes over Homer’s.

entities.name: Thonis
entities.body: The warden of the Canobic mouth who arrested Alexander’s servants and reported him to Proteus.

entities.name: Rhampsinitos
entities.body: The rich king whose treasury a mason’s two sons robbed through a movable stone — the best story in Book 2 — and who ended by marrying his daughter to the thief.

entities.name: Cheops
entities.body: The king who shut the temples, set the whole people to work on his pyramid for twenty years, and sold his own daughter’s favours to pay for it.

entities.name: Chephren
entities.body: Cheops’s brother and successor, who ruled in the same manner for fifty-six years; the Egyptians will not willingly say either brother’s name.

entities.name: Mykerinos
entities.body: Cheops’s son, who opened the temples again and gave the people back their lives — and was told by the oracle that he had six years to live because Egypt was meant to suffer a hundred and fifty. He answered by lighting lamps and living the nights as well.

entities.name: Asychis
entities.body: The king who made a law that a man might borrow on his father’s corpse, and built a pyramid of brick with an inscription telling it not to compare itself with the stone ones.

entities.name: Anysis
entities.body: The blind king of the city of the same name, who fled into the marshes when the Ethiopians came and hid there fifty years on a floating island of ash and earth.

entities.name: Sabacos
entities.body: The Ethiopian who ruled Egypt for fifty years without putting anyone to death, and left because of a dream rather than wait for it to come true.

entities.name: Sethos
entities.body: The priest of Hephaistos who despised the warrior class and was saved from Sennacherib by field-mice that ate the Assyrians’ bowstrings overnight.

entities.name: Psammetichos
entities.body: One of the twelve kings, driven out and returned with the bronze men the oracle promised; he reunited Egypt, opened it to Greek traders, and shut two children away with a mute shepherd to find out which language came first. The two editions spell him Psammetichos and Psammetichus.

entities.name: Necos
entities.body: Psammetichos’s son, who began the canal to the Red Sea, gave it up when the oracle warned him, and sent Phoenicians to sail round Libya. The older translation spells him Necos; he is also the father Sabacos killed.

entities.name: Psammis
entities.body: Necos’s son, who reigned six years, invaded Ethiopia, and gave the Eleians the obvious answer about their own games.

entities.name: Apries
entities.body: Psammis’s son, the most prosperous king but one until his army went over to Amasis; he was kept alive in his own palace and then handed to the Egyptians, who strangled him.

entities.name: Patarbemis
entities.body: The man of reputation Apries sent to fetch Amasis back, and whose ears and nose Apries cut off when he came back without him — which lost Apries the rest of his subjects.

entities.name: Ladice
entities.body: The Cyrenaean woman Amasis married, who prayed to Aphrodite when he could not come to her and afterwards sent the goddess a statue.

entities.name: Amyrtaios
entities.body: The only man in seven hundred years to find the floating island in the marshes where Anysis had hidden.

entities.name: Rhodopis
entities.body: The Thracian courtesan the Greeks credit with the third pyramid — wrongly, Herodotus says, since she lived generations later. She spent a tenth of her fortune on iron roasting-spits at Delphi.

entities.name: Iadmon
entities.body: The Samian who owned Rhodopis, and Aesop before her.

entities.name: Aesop
entities.body: The fable-maker, named here as Rhodopis’s fellow-slave, for whose killing the Delphians had to pay compensation.

entities.name: Charaxos
entities.body: The man of Mytilene who bought Rhodopis’s freedom at great expense, and was mocked for it in his sister’s poetry.

entities.name: Sappho
entities.body: Charaxos’s sister, named as the lyric poet who made a song about what her brother had spent his money on.

entities.name: Etearchus
entities.body: King of the Ammonians, who told the Nasamonians’ story of the five young men who crossed the desert and came to a city of small black men beside a river full of crocodiles.

entities.name: Archander
entities.body: Son-in-law of Danaus, after whom a city in the Delta is named; Herodotus doubts the name is Egyptian at all.

entities.name: Hecataeus
entities.body: The historian who traced his own descent to a god in the sixteenth generation, and was shown three hundred and forty-five wooden statues at Thebes to correct him.

entities.name: Menelaus
entities.body: Helen’s husband, who came to Egypt for her after Troy fell, got her back from Proteus, and repaid the Egyptians by sacrificing two of their children for a wind.

entities.name: Hector
entities.body: Priam’s elder and abler son, whose existence Herodotus uses as the proof that Troy would have given Helen up if it had had her.

entities.name: Homer
entities.body: Whom Herodotus supposes to have invented the river Ocean, to have known the Egyptian version of Helen and set it aside as less suitable for poetry, and to have lived four hundred years before his own day.

entities.name: Hesiod
entities.body: Named with Homer as the pair who made the Greeks their theogony, gave the gods their titles and described their forms.

entities.name: Perseus
entities.body: Whose watchtower stands on the Egyptian coast and whose sandal turns up at Chemmis; the people there say he was theirs, being descended from Danaus.

entities.name: Danaus
entities.body: Of Chemmis, from whom the people there trace Perseus; his daughters brought the rite of the Thesmophoria out of Egypt. The two editions spell him Danaus and Danaos.

entities.name: Lynceus
entities.body: Named with Danaus as a man of Chemmis who sailed to Greece.

entities.name: Amphitryon
entities.body: Heracles’s mortal father — of Egyptian descent, the Egyptians say, which is why the Greeks are wrong about which Heracles is older.

entities.name: Alcmene
entities.body: Heracles’s mother, named with Amphitryon in the same argument.

entities.name: Melampus
entities.body: Son of Amytheon, who Herodotus thinks brought the rite of Dionysus into Greece from Egypt, having learned it from Cadmus and the Phoenicians.

entities.name: Amytheon
entities.body: Melampus’s father.

entities.name: Cadmus
entities.body: The Phoenician from whom Melampus is supposed to have learned the Egyptian rites. The two editions spell him Cadmus and Cadmos.

entities.name: Semele
entities.body: Cadmus’s daughter, the mother of the Greek Dionysus — sixteen hundred years after the Egyptian one, on Herodotus’s reckoning.

entities.name: Penelope
entities.body: Of whom the Greeks say Pan was born, and Hermes — eight hundred years after the Egyptian Pan.

entities.name: Linus
entities.body: The song the Egyptians call Maneros, sung in Phoenicia and Cyprus under other names, and the one song the Egyptians have.

entities.name: Danae
entities.body: Perseus’s mother, named in the Chemmite genealogy.

entities.name: Hephaestus
entities.body: The god the Greeks call Hephaestus and the Egyptians Ptah, whose priests at Memphis are Herodotus’s main informants; his temple is the one every king adds to. The two editions spell him Hephaestus and Hephaistos.

entities.name: Isis
entities.body: Whose figure is a woman with cow’s horns, and who is Demeter in Greek. Cows are sacred to her and are never sacrificed.

entities.name: Osiris
entities.body: Isis’s fellow — Dionysus in Greek — whose sufferings are represented at Saïs on the night the Egyptians call the Lamps.

entities.name: Dionysus
entities.body: Osiris under his Greek name, whose rites Melampus is supposed to have brought to Greece, and who with Demeter rules the world below in the Egyptian account. The two editions spell him Dionysus and Dionysos.

entities.name: Demeter
entities.body: Isis under her Greek name, ruler with Dionysus of the world below.

entities.name: Leto
entities.body: Honoured at Buto, where the floating island is and where the oracle spoke; in the Egyptian story she was Apollo’s nurse, not his mother.

entities.name: Artemis
entities.body: Honoured at Bubastis with the greatest festival in Egypt; in the Egyptian account she is the daughter of Dionysus and Isis.

entities.name: Ares
entities.body: Honoured at Papremis, where the festival is a real fight with clubs at the temple gate.

entities.name: Pan
entities.body: One of the eight oldest gods in the Egyptian reckoning, painted and carved with a goat’s face and a he-goat’s legs; the Mendesians will not sacrifice goats because of him.

entities.name: Hermes
entities.body: Whose images the Greeks make as they do because they learned it from the Pelasgians, not from the Egyptians; and whom the Greeks call Pan’s father.

entities.name: Poseidon
entities.body: A god the Egyptians say they do not know, and who came to the Greeks from the Libyans.

entities.name: The Dioscuri
entities.body: Named with Poseidon among the gods the Egyptians say they have never heard of.

entities.name: Ammon
entities.body: The god of the oracle in the Libyan desert, whose name is the Egyptian name for Zeus; his image is a ram, and that is why the Thebans will not sacrifice sheep.

entities.name: Helios
entities.body: The Sun, honoured at Heliopolis; the Egyptians say he once rose where he now sets, twice over, within written memory.

entities.name: Typhon
entities.body: Set under his Greek name, whom Horus deposed to become the last divine king of Egypt.

entities.name: The Ethiopians
entities.body: Egypt’s neighbours up the Nile, whose king Sabacos held Egypt for fifty years, and among whom the Deserters settled beyond Meroe.

entities.name: The Libyans
entities.body: Whose land runs west from Egypt; the Marea and Apis people claimed to be Libyans and not Egyptians so as to eat cow’s flesh, and were told by the oracle that all the Nile waters is Egypt.

entities.name: The Colchians
entities.body: Whom Herodotus judges to be Egyptian by descent on three grounds — their skin, their hair, and the fact that they circumcise.

entities.name: The Nasamonians
entities.body: The Libyan people of the Syrtis whose five adventurous young men crossed the desert and found a city of small dark men by a great river running east.

entities.name: The Ammonians
entities.body: Etearchus’s people, at the oracle of Ammon; colonists, Herodotus says, from both Egypt and Ethiopia.

entities.name: The Mendesians
entities.body: Who count Pan among the eight oldest gods, keep goats sacred, and have the story about the he-goat that is not to be repeated.

entities.name: The Samothracians
entities.body: Who perform the mysteries of the Cabeiri, learned from the Pelasgians who used to live on the island.

entities.name: The Eleians
entities.body: Who came to Psammis boasting that their arrangement of the Olympic games was the justest in the world, and were told to let strangers compete if they meant it.

entities.name: The Calasirians
entities.body: One of the two Egyptian warrior classes, with their own districts and their twelve aruras of tax-free land.

entities.name: The Hermotybians
entities.body: The other Egyptian warrior class, named with the Calasirians.

entities.name: The Celts
entities.body: Beyond the Pillars of Heracles, at whose country the Ister begins.

entities.name: The Trojans
entities.body: Who, Herodotus argues, would have given Helen back if they had had her, since they were losing their lives for her by the day.

entities.name: The Cilicians
entities.body: Named as the people whose land Cilicia is, in the argument about what makes a country.
